To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the growth response to elevated atmospheric CO2 is amplified when plant growth is limited by water, but is reduced when growth is limited by nitrogen.

(1) plant productivity at elevated CO2 is maximised when leaf [N], LAI and stomal conductance are at an optimum, (2) the optimum for leaf [CO2], LAI and LAI is shifted to lower values at elevated CO2, and (3) this shift in the optimum is amplified under water-limited conditions, but is reduced under nitrogen-limited conditions.
the response of plant growth to elevated CO2 can be understood in terms of a model of the annual water-nitrogen-carbon economy of a tree.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the optimisation hypothesis, which is a simple and general explanation for the observed effects of CO2 enrichment on stomatal conductance ([g(s)]), leaf [N], LAI and the growth response to elevated [CO2].

the physiological basis for the observed response of plant productivity to elevated CO2, and we suggest that the optimisation hypothesis provides a useful framework for understanding the effects of CO2 on the carbon, nitrogen and water economy of plants.

the physiological mechanisms underlying plant-growth response and the optimisation hypothesis provides a simple explanation for the contrasting growth response to CO2 enrichment in years with contrasting water and N supply.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the response to elevated [CO2] is amplified under water-limiting conditions, but reduced under N-limiting conditions, because of the physiological effects of stomatal closure and leaf [N]-decline, respectively, and because these effects are more pronounced at low than at high water and N supply, respectively.

plant growth response to elevated [CO2] is greater under water limitation than under nitrogen limitation because the photosynthetic response to elevated [ CO2] is more pronounced under low stomatal conductance (i.e. low transpiration rate) than under low leaf [N].

the growth response to elevated atmospheric [CO2] is enhanced by a decline in stomatal conductance under water limitation, and is reduced under nitrogen limitation, because the photosynthetic rate is more sensitive to [CO 2] when the stomata are partially closed, and less sensitive to [C O 2] when leaf [N] is low.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the growth response to elevated [CO2] is amplified when water limitation reduces stomatal conductance below the optimal value for the ambient CO2 concentration, but reduced when N limitation reduces leaf [N] below the optimal value.

the growth response to elevated [CO2] is enhanced by conditions that reduce stomatal conductance (such as water limitation) and reduced by conditions that reduce leaf nitrogen concentration (such as nitrogen limitation).

the growth response of trees to elevated CO2 in a dry, N-rich year is greater than in a wet, N-poor year, because in a dry year stomatal conductance is reduced and leaf [N ] is increased, but in a wet year stomatal conductances are similar and leaf [N]'s are lower at elevated CO2.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in the context of the optimisation hypothesis, plant-growth response (R) to elevated CO2 can be expressed in terms of the ratio of the optimum stomatal conductance under ambient and elevated CO2 (g*o/ g*o), multiplied by the ratio of the optimal leaf [N] under ambient and elevated [CO2] (N*o/N*o).

optimisation of plant growth in terms of the trade-off between LAIs and stomatal conductances constrained by water supply and between LAIs and leaf [N]'s constrained by N supply provides a simple explanation for the contrasting growth response to CO2 enrichment under water limitation versus nitrogen limitation.
the response of plant growth to elevated CO2 can be understood by optimisation of the annual carbon, nitrogen and water economy.
